opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say it's gone faster than I expected, though maybe not in the way I would have predicted. Back in 2019, when GPT-2 came out, I thought it was impressive. It could write coherent paragraphs, and that was surprising. But I don't think I appreciated how far just scaling up that recipe would take us. I was more in the camp of thinking we'd need a lot of new algorithmic ideas, maybe more of a focus on RL and agents interacting with environments, before we got something that felt generally useful.

What actually happened is that pretraining on huge amounts of text gave you this incredibly rich base of knowledge and capabilities. Then the post-training work, RLHF, instruction tuning, and so on, turned out to be a relatively cheap way to unlock that and make it usable. I didn't anticipate that the combination would get you to something like ChatGPT as quickly as it did.

That said, some things have been slower than I would've guessed. Long-horizon tasks, where a model has to carry out a coherent project over hours or days, recover from its own mistakes, and keep track of what it's doing, have lagged behind the raw knowledge and short-form reasoning. The models are brilliant in some respects and still oddly brittle in others.

So if you'd shown me today's systems in 2019, I think I'd have been pretty shocked and would've guessed it was further out. But the shape of progress is a bit different from what I imagined. It's much more "scale plus a good post-training recipe" and less "invent a whole new paradigm" than I expected.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Schulman underestimated how far scaling would go and expected more new algorithmic ideas, but it does not distinguish confidence in scaling and pretraining from a belief that they would revolutionize everything.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions GPT-2 and ChatGPT but does not identify GPT-3 as the point when Schulman redirected his research toward language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Around the time of GPT-2, I think my expectation was that things would get better in a sort of gradual, incremental way. We had this scaling story starting to take shape, and the GPT-2 results were a big update that language modeling at scale could give you these surprisingly general capabilities. But I don't think I would have predicted the specific trajectory we've seen.

A couple of things surprised me. One is just how far pure scaling of pretraining went. There was a lot of debate back then about whether you'd hit a wall, whether you needed fundamentally new architectures or some kind of grounding to get real reasoning. And it turned out that you could just keep going and the models kept picking up more and more. The second thing is how well the post-training side worked, RLHF and related methods. Going from a raw language model that's hard to use to something people actually want to talk to was a bigger jump than I expected in terms of its practical impact. I think ChatGPT taking off the way it did caught a lot of us off guard, not because the underlying capability was so far beyond what we had, but because the usefulness of a conversational interface was underrated.

On the other hand, some things have been slower than I'd have guessed. In 2019 if you'd told me we'd have models that could write decent code and pass hard exams, I probably would have assumed they'd also be reliably doing long autonomous tasks, acting as real agents. And that's been harder. The gap between being impressive in a single interaction and being robust over many steps without supervision is bigger than I appreciated. So overall I'd say progress has been faster than my median expectation, but shaped differently, with capabilities coming in a sort of jagged way rather than uniformly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says GPT-2 strengthened the scaling story and showed surprising general capabilities, while Schulman expected gradual progress and did not predict the trajectory that followed.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention GPT-3 or say it prompted Schulman to redirect his research toward language models.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s been faster than I expected, although my expectations in 2019 weren’t very precise. GPT-2 was already a sign that you could get surprisingly general behavior just by training a language model on a lot of text. But it was hard to tell how far that would go. Would scaling keep producing substantial improvements, or would we run into some limitation that required a new idea?

What’s surprised me is how much mileage we’ve gotten out of essentially the same basic recipe. The models have become much better at coding, following instructions, and working through problems, without needing to replace the underlying approach.

I’d also separate the progress in capabilities from the progress in making those capabilities useful. With GPT-2, you had this interesting text generator, but it wasn’t an assistant you could reliably ask to do something. Getting models to follow instructions made a big difference in how people could interact with them. I think that transformation would have been difficult for me to fully anticipate in 2019.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it was unclear whether scaling would continue to improve models, but it does not distinguish confidence in scaling and pretraining from belief that it would revolutionize everything.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions GPT-2 and later model improvements, but does not identify GPT-3 as prompting Schulman to redirect his research toward language models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest surprise has been how far you can get with the same basic recipe. In 2019, it seemed plausible that scaling up language models would keep improving them, but it wasn’t clear how far that would take us—or whether we’d need some major new idea to get much more general capabilities.

And it’s hard to say what you expected, because there’s a difference between thinking something might happen and actually anticipating what it will feel like. You can believe the models will get much better at writing code, and still be surprised when you can sit down and have a useful back-and-forth with one about a programming problem.

So I’d say the direction was less surprising than the extent. Scaling worked remarkably well, and then post-training made those capabilities much easier to access. The combination has been pretty striking.

r001.rationale: It says continued improvement from scaling seemed plausible, while the extent of progress and its general capabilities were uncertain. That conveys confidence in the direction without expecting a sweeping transformation.
